reasons: No test is visible in this file to confirm that ids stay stable over time.
The design relies on 20 hex characters being collision-free, which is not checked here.

terms.meaning: A fixed method that turns any text into a fixed-length code, so the same input always gives the same code.
The result of running text through a method such as SHA-256.
A standard way of writing accented or combined characters so the same text compares equal.
An identifier whose internal parts are not meant to be read; it is only used to match things.
The named position a part occupies within its asset.
A name that picks out one specific asset among several of the same kind.

depends_on: Python standard library: hashlib, json, unicodedata

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports for hashing and text
sections.what: Brings in the tools for hashing, JSON text and Unicode normalisation. Nothing visible to the user happens here.
sections.why: Likely reason: the standard library provides a stable way to build fingerprints of text.

sections.name: _identity
sections.title: Core id builder
sections.what: Makes one id from a kind name and a set of key texts. It normalises each key, rejects blank or very long keys, hashes the group and keeps the first 20 hex characters after a kind prefix.
sections.why: The code comments say case and opaque ids are preserved on purpose, so merging two similar names is always an explicit decision by the caller.
sections.watch_out: Changing the normalisation or the hash length changes every id in every saved file.

sections.name: asset_identity
sections.title: Id for a physical asset
sections.what: Makes the id for one physical asset from the project id, the asset key and the instance key. The id stays the same while evidence and geometry change.
sections.why: The docstring says an asset's key and slot persist as the evidence evolves, so references to the asset keep working.
sections.watch_out: The asset key and instance key must stay the same across versions, because any change makes a new asset.

sections.name: part_identity
sections.title: Id for one part of an asset
sections.what: Makes the id for one part inside an asset from the asset id and the part's semantic slot.
sections.why: Likely reason: parts are referenced by slot name so the same part keeps its id across rebuilds.
sections.watch_out: Renaming a semantic slot creates a new part id and breaks any saved reference to the old one.

sections.name: inventory_subject
sections.title: Id for an inventory count
sections.what: Makes the id for a count of one asset class within a project, independent of the individual assets' other claims.
sections.why: The docstring says the count is a class-level claim that stands on its own.
sections.watch_out: The id depends only on project and asset key, so two counts with the same key collide by design.

sections.name: part_property_subject
sections.title: Id for a property claim
sections.what: Makes the id for a claim that a specific dimension or property applies either to a whole class or to one named asset instance. The docstring warns that a raw dimension is not automatically assigned to a model axis, and creating the claim needs a review.
sections.why: The docstring says claims need reviewed applicability and retained source basis, so the id is the anchor for that record.
sections.watch_out: Adding or dropping the instance key changes the id, so a claim moved between class and instance scope becomes a different claim.

summary: Creates stable, opaque text ids for assets, parts, inventory counts and property claims by hashing their key names.
purpose: Keeps references between saved parts of the model valid even when source files change order, version or wording of their bytes.
why: The docstring states the ids are independent of source bytes, version and order. This is the stated reason for the design.
how: Each public function joins its key texts into a fixed group. The shared helper normalises each key to a standard Unicode form, rejects blank or very long keys, serialises the group as JSON, hashes it with SHA-256, keeps the first 20 hex characters and adds a kind prefix.
inputs: Text keys such as the project id, asset key, instance key, semantic slot and parameter name.
outputs: Text ids such as an asset, part, inventory or property id, each with a kind prefix and 20 hex characters.
risks: Changing a key, the normalisation, the key order or the length of the hash changes every affected id and breaks saved references. Keys are case-sensitive on purpose, so spelling differences create new ids. Blank or over-long keys raise errors.
debug: If references break after an update, compare the ids produced for the same inputs before and after. Check whether a key's spelling, case or order changed. For an identity error, check the key length and whether any key is blank.
